claims.text: The initial Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is a single-phase BCC material.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the initial alloy indicate dendritic and interdendritic compositional micro-segregation.
The initial alloy has significantly lower room-temperature fracture strain than theoretical predictions.
Adding approximately 4 at.% Cr induces a multicomponent Laves phase in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The Cr-modified alloy contains a C14 or C15 Laves phase coexisting with a BCC matrix.
The Laves phase occupies approximately 4 vol% of the Cr-modified alloy.
The Laves phase forms a reticulated, interconnected morphology concentrated at interdendritic regions.
Cr addition contracts the lattice parameter of the BCC matrix.
The interconnected Laves phase forces cracks onto tortuous paths through crack deflection and branching, increasing fracture area and energy dissipation.
Cr-induced BCC lattice contraction increases lattice friction or Peierls stress through solid-solution hardening.
The proposed solid-solution hardening delays necking and promotes uniform plastic deformation before fracture.
Cr addition increases room-temperature fracture strain relative to the Cr-free alloy.
Cr addition increases yield strength relative to the Cr-free alloy.
The modified alloy's fracture surface will show crack deflection along the Laves network rather than brittle cleavage along interdendritic boundaries.
The low fracture strain of the Cr-free baseline is caused by brittle crack propagation through micro-segregated interdendritic regions.
If the BCC lattice parameter expands or remains unchanged after Cr addition, the proposed solid-solution-hardening mechanism is invalidated.
Casting followed by homogenization ensures an equilibrium phase distribution while retaining a focus on secondary-phase formation at interdendritic regions.
Substrate or cooling-rate effects may determine whether the Laves phase adopts the C14 or C15 structure.
Processing the Cr-containing and Cr-free batches at identical cooling rates minimizes differences in segregation.
